title: Colonel Sanders Sold KFC For $2M. It Resold For $285M

beats.say: You could sell for two million, then watch buyers resell it for two hundred eighty five million.
beats.visual: one small paper bucket of fried chicken on a stone pedestal beside a colossal mountain of identical buckets rising into clouds, extreme wide shot, no lettering, no people

beats.say: Harland Sanders sold fried chicken from a roadside restaurant in Corbin, Kentucky.
beats.visual: a lone timber roadside cafe with a glowing paper lantern by its door beside a narrow country road at dusk, low angle from the ground, no people

beats.say: In nineteen fifty two, at sixty two, he began franchising his recipe.
beats.visual: a heavy cast iron pressure fryer on a charcoal flame with steam curling from its valve, macro with razor focus, no people

beats.say: A planned interstate would bypass Corbin, so he auctioned his business for seventy five thousand dollars.
beats.visual: an aerial view of a broad new road curving around a sleepy mountain village and leaving its single lane untouched, morning mist, no people

beats.say: He later wrote of a one hundred five dollar Social Security check arriving every month.
beats.visual: a thin plain paper envelope tied with string on a windowsill while rain streaks the glass behind it, shallow focus, no people

beats.say: By nineteen sixty four, more than six hundred restaurants were franchised.
beats.visual: a long village lane lined with hundreds of identical glowing paper lanterns fading into the dusk, long lens compression, no people

beats.say: That year, at seventy three, he sold his interest to investors for two million dollars.
beats.visual: two pairs of hands passing a closed red lacquer box across a tatami mat, overhead view, faces out of frame, no people

beats.say: In July nineteen seventy one, the company was sold to Heublein for two hundred eighty five million dollars.
beats.visual: a towering stone castle keep rising above a sea of small tiled rooftops, worm's-eye view up its walls, no people

beats.say: Here is the part nobody tells you. The rags to riches meme skips that he had franchised since sixty two.
beats.visual: the cut cross section of an ancient cedar stump with dense growth rings, macro, soft rain on the bark, no people

beats.say: The honest catch: the buyers grew it to over thirty five hundred restaurants, so that gap is not simply his loss.
beats.visual: a bamboo ladder leaning against a tall persimmon tree with one rung cracked through, looking up from the roots, no people

beats.say: The lesson is about trade-offs. Selling a business swaps its future growth for cash today.
beats.visual: a balance scale holding a green seedling in one pan and a small mound of rice in the other, silhouette against a glowing paper screen, no people

beats.say: This is a story, not a plan. Your situation and risks are your own.
beats.visual: a pair of straw sandals set neatly on a stone step at a quiet inn entrance in falling snow, close eye level, no people

beats.say: Follow for the money rules school never taught you.
beats.visual: a white crane lifting off a still misty pond at first light, extreme wide silhouette, no people

description: Colonel Harland Sanders began franchising his chicken in 1952. In 1964, with more than 600 franchised restaurants, he sold his interest for $2 million. In July 1971 the company sold to Heublein for $285 million, after the buyers grew it past 3,500 restaurants, so the gap is not simply his loss. A story, not a plan. Educational only, not financial advice.
first_comment: Would you sell a business you built for cash today, or keep the risk and the growth? Educational only, not financial advice.

facts.claim: Sanders began franchising his chicken in 1952, at age 62, starting with Pete Harman in Salt Lake City, Utah; the viral rags-to-riches meme about starting at 65 was rated false
facts.basis: AAP FactCheck, 2021-10-19, 'Barely a nugget of truth in Colonel Sanders rags-to-riches meme'; Wikipedia (Colonel Sanders)

facts.claim: Sanders wrote that he had a $105 Social Security check coming in every month
facts.basis: Sanders's own words quoted in AAP FactCheck, 2021-10-19; Encyclopedia.com (Colonel Sanders biography)

facts.claim: With the interstate bypass of Corbin, Kentucky planned, Sanders sold his business at auction for $75,000 (1956)
facts.basis: AAP FactCheck, 2021-10-19 (quoting Sanders); Encyclopedia.com (Colonel Sanders biography)

facts.claim: In 1964, with more than 600 franchised outlets, Sanders sold his interest in Kentucky Fried Chicken for $2 million to investors led by John Y. Brown Jr. and Jack Massey; he was 73
facts.basis: Biography.com (Colonel Harland Sanders); Wikipedia (KFC, citing Smith 2011); AOL/Benzinga report on the sale

facts.claim: In July 1971 the company was sold to Heublein for $285 million, with more than 3,500 franchised and company-owned restaurants
facts.basis: Wikipedia (KFC, citing Barmash, New York Times, 1971); AOL report citing KFC's history

caption: Colonel Sanders sold his interest in KFC for $2 million in 1964. In 1971 the company sold for $285 million, after the buyers grew it past 3,500 restaurants. A story, not a plan. Educational content, not financial advice.
